verdict.winner: Solar panels win on output per dollar and roof area; solar shingles win on roof-integrated appearance.
verdict.reasoning: Solar panels beat solar shingles when output per dollar leads: panels reach 20-22% efficiency at ~$2.50-$4.00 per watt and need ~250 square feet for a 6-kW system, versus shingles' 14-18% at ~$3.50-$8.00 per watt over ~360 square feet (per SolarReviews and EnergySage).
verdict.alternate: Solar shingles beat solar panels when a roof needs replacement and integration leads: BIPV shingles replace the roof covering in one project, while CertainTeed Solstice and similar lines cannot go over an existing roof (per the DOE and CertainTeed).

keyFacts: Solar panels run 20-22% efficient versus solar shingles' 14-18% (BIPV range 13-23%) (per SolarReviews).
Solar panels install at ~$2.50-$4.00 per watt versus solar shingles' ~$3.50-$8.00 per watt, roughly 1.5-2x the per-watt cost (per EnergySage and SolarReviews).
Installed cost per square foot is $7-$10 for solar panels versus $21-$25 for solar shingles (per SolarTech Online).
A 6-kW system needs ~250 square feet of solar panels versus ~360 square feet of solar shingles (per SolarReviews).

Solar shingles are building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) that replace the roof covering, while solar panels are building-applied photovoltaics (BAPV) rack-mounted above an existing roof (per the DOE and IEA-PVPS).

Named BIPV solar-shingle products: GAF Energy Timberline Solar ES 2 (57 W per energy shingle, ~16.7 W per square foot), Tesla Solar Roof (72 W per active glass tile), CertainTeed Solstice (70 W, 19.85% module efficiency), and SunTegra (105-114 W) (per the manufacturers' datasheets).
Solar panels are crystalline-silicon modules of roughly 350-470 watts (~400 W common), racked above the deck (per NREL).
Solar panels degrade a median ~0.5% per year to ~85-88% of rated output by year 25-30 (per NREL).
Solar shingles carry a ~25-year power warranty (~84.8-85% at year 25); solar panels carry a ~25-year warranty (~85-88% at year 25-30) (per the manufacturers and NREL).

Solar panels attach through flashed lag-bolt rail feet whose upper flange tucks under the upslope shingle course so water sheds onto intact shingles; solar shingles are field-integrated and nailed in (per NRCA guidance and the DOE).
Flush-mounted solar shingles run hotter, trimming output ~0.3-0.5% per degree C above 25 degrees C (per WattBuild and NREL's thermal coefficient).

Both solar shingles and solar panels meet NJ-relevant wind, hail, and fire ratings: BIPV shingles list UL 7103 certification, UL 790 Class A fire, UL 2218 Class 4 hail, and ASTM D3161 Class F wind (per the manufacturers' datasheets).
GAF Energy Timberline Solar lists Class A fire, Class 4 hail, and 130-mph wind on a pitch of 2:12 or steeper; SunTegra lists 130-mph wind with UL 2218 Class 4 (per GAF Energy and SunTegra).

Solar panels must meet NEC 690.12 rapid shutdown: conductors fall to <=30 volts outside and <=80 volts inside the array boundary within 30 seconds; the module-plus-mounting-plus-roof assembly carries the UL 790 fire class (per the NEC and UL).
Solar panels shade the roof covering but do not extend its service life as established fact; any quantified roof-life extension is marketing, not a verified figure (per NRCA guidance).

On a flat commercial roof, solar panels mount on ballasted non-penetrating racking (weighted by blocks over a protection pad) or on mechanically attached flashed anchors, with uplift and ballast governed by ASCE 7 (per NRCA and SPRI).
Solar shingles rarely fit commercial buildings because BIPV is a sloped roof-covering replacement, leaving the higher per-watt cost without the integration payoff (per the DOE and SolarTech Online).
njContext: The NJ SuSI program pays a fixed per-MWh SREC-II over a 15-year term, set at registration by the NJ Board of Public Utilities; both solar shingles and solar panels are eligible (per NJBPU).

NJ net metering credits both systems identically: N.J.S.A. 48:3-87 requires full retail (1:1) credit for exports up to the customer's annual usage, with net annual surplus settled at the wholesale avoided-cost rate (per the statute and NJBPU).

The federal residential solar credit no longer applies to either system completed in 2026: the IRS Section 25D credit was 30% for systems completed through December 31, 2025, then repealed under P.L. 119-21 (per the IRS); a homeowner confirms current incentives with a tax professional.

High-efficiency solar panels at 20-22% extract more output from the limited south-facing roof area common on densely built Essex County lots, since fewer modules reach a target system size (per SolarReviews and GreenLancer).
Solar shingles suit integration-driven Essex County houses (flush look during a reroof); solar panels suit output-driven ones (more watts per dollar) (per the DOE and SolarReviews).

An industry rule of thumb re-roofs first when the roof outlasts neither the ~25-30-year panels nor the array, to avoid removing and reinstalling the array mid-roof; the panel-life figure is per NREL, the re-roof-first timing is an industry rule of thumb with no named standard.
positioning: Newark Quality Roofing is a registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor (N.J.S.A. 56:8-136), insured, offering a free written estimate. For this solar comparison NQR handles the roofing side only, not the solar design: mount flashing and flashed rail attachments, ASCE 7 wind/ballast load on the assembly, the re-roof-before-solar timing decision when a roof has limited remaining life, and NEC 690.12 / fire-rating coordination with the solar installer. Warranty framing is honestly two-part: a manufacturer material/power warranty plus a contractor written workmanship warranty on the roofing work; never claim certification tiers (no Master Elite / SELECT ShingleMaster / Tesla-certified). All cost, efficiency, and rating figures trace to named aggregators, manufacturers, and standards, not to NQR.

buyersGuide.h1: Which Is Better: Solar Shingles vs Solar Panels?
buyersGuide.directAnswerThesis: Solar panels are better for output per dollar (20-22% efficient, ~$2.50-$4.00/watt, ~250 sq ft per 6 kW); solar shingles win only when a roof needs full replacement and roof-integrated looks decide it (per SolarReviews and EnergySage).
sectionAngles: Which rooftop solar costs less and produces more per dollar in NJ? (panels' 20-22% at $2.50-$4.00/watt and ~250 sq ft vs shingles' 14-18% at $3.50-$8.00/watt and ~360 sq ft, per SolarReviews/EnergySage)

How do NJ incentives and code shape the decision in 2026? (SuSI SREC-II 15-year term and N.J.S.A. 48:3-87 1:1 net metering apply to both; the IRS Section 25D 30% credit was repealed for systems completed after Dec 31, 2025 under P.L. 119-21, per NJBPU and the IRS)

When does roof condition decide between integration and add-on? (shingles pair with a full reroof and cannot go over an existing roof per CertainTeed/DOE; panels add to a roof with remaining service life, re-roofing first when the roof outlasts neither the ~25-30-yr panels nor the array)

expertPicks.h1: What Do NJ Roofers Recommend for Solar Shingles vs Solar Panels?
expertPicks.directAnswerThesis: The evidence favors solar panels on a sound existing roof and solar shingles only when a full reroof is already due; a registered NJ Home Improvement Contractor coordinates flashing, ASCE 7 load, and re-roof timing, not the solar design.
sectionAngles: What do the roofing standards favor on attachment and waterproofing? (panels use flashed rail feet whose flange tucks under the upslope course so water sheds onto intact shingles, per NRCA/DOE; shingles nail in as the covering and the manufacturer warranty governs leaks under the array)

Which installation-quality and code factors decide long-term performance? (UL 790 Class A fire, UL 2218 Class 4 hail, ASTM D3161 / 130-mph wind ratings on BIPV per manufacturer datasheets; NEC 690.12 rapid shutdown to <=30V/<=80V; ASCE 7 uplift/ballast on flat commercial roofs per NRCA/SPRI)

What is the most common homeowner mistake, and how does re-roof timing avoid it? (putting panels on a roof that will outlast neither the ~25-30-yr panels nor the array forces a costly mid-life remove-and-reinstall; an industry rule of thumb re-roofs first, panel life per NREL, no named standard for the timing)
